book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

chapters.file: ch04 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch07 - And If You Listen Very Hard . ..md
chapters.relation: Editor Scott Calef's introduction argues that the critics who dismissed Led Zeppelin as hype, blues thieves, and purveyors of mere excess were wrong: Page and Jones had long apprenticeships, Plant spread asphalt while struggling, and the band released four albums in two years while touring nonstop. It contends the band invites philosophy because Page (occultism, the Hermit tarot figure on Led Zeppelin IV) and Plant (mythology, the feather-of-truth symbol) were serious spiritual seekers, and because Zep's music resists tidy genre categories just as philosophy challenges our everyday categories of creativity, recognition, and value. It closes by invoking Aristotle's claim that philosophy begins in wonder, prompted by Plant's 'it makes me wonder' in 'Stairway to Heaven'.

chapters.file: ch08 - From Low to High Culture Where’s That Confounded Bridge.md
chapters.relation: John Stone-Mediatore argues that Led Zeppelin's music, especially in concert, is a quintessential experience of the sublime. He applies Burke's catalogue of sublime qualities (loudness, darkness, rudeness, the artificial infinite) to Bonham's cavernous drum sound on 'When the Levee Breaks', Page's rough overdriven tone and 'sloppy' technique, and the dissonant mandolin intro and nocturnal imagery of 'The Battle of Evermore'; Longinus's inspired, thunderbolt-like genius explains Plant's overnight writing of the 'Stairway to Heaven' lyrics at Headley Grange. Kant's account of imagination, understanding, and reason then shows why the impossible stairway to heaven, 'our shadows taller than our soul', and 'when all are one and one is all' frustrate concepts and delight us through reason's superiority. The chapter concludes that once rock attains the sublime, the high/low culture distinction is mere aesthetic snobbery.

chapters.file: ch09 - Bring It On Home to You.md
chapters.relation: Jeanette Bicknell argues that the two classic models of creativity—Plato's Ion, where the rhapsode is a divinely possessed conduit, and Kant's solitary genius who issues new rules—cannot explain a four-piece rock band, since both are individualistic, purely mental, and end in mystery. Her positive account uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind (Page describes his guitar as 'an extension of you', instruments and notation as cognitive props) and Keith Sawyer's collaborative emergence: Zeppelin's creativity happened in rehearsal and performance, as with the stairwell-recorded drum groove of 'When the Levee Breaks' that framed every later musical decision. The transformation of Joan Baez's 'Babe, I'm Gonna Leave You' into a whisper-to-cry hard-rock template shows the band creating something no member could have produced or predicted alone.

Theodore Gracyk asks whether Zeppelin's uncredited borrowings—Willie Dixon's 'You Need Love' into 'Whole Lotta Love', Spirit's 'Taurus' into 'Stairway to Heaven', Jake Holmes's 'I'm Confused' into 'Dazed and Confused'—undermine their status as an authentic rock band whose value supposedly rests on sincere self-expression and original songwriting. Using Hanslick's thought experiment as staged by Little Roger and the Goosebumps's 'Gilligan's Island (Stairway)' parody and Handel's recycling of his own music into the Messiah, he argues a song's expressive power comes from the interaction of words and music (guarding against the fallacies of division and composition), and that by itself music is neither angry nor spiritual. Since Zeppelin's instrumental arrangements diverge radically from their sources and the lawsuits turned on Plant's lyrics, the chapter concludes that transformation, not narrow originality, grounds their genius—so the rock-versus-pop authenticity standard must be loosened.

chapters.file: ch11 - Tell Me No Lies, Make Me a Happy Man.md
chapters.relation: Luke Dick gives a phenomenological analysis of what it is to be moved by 'Black Dog', introducing affectivity through a fantasy in which a stranger insulting Zeppelin instantly provokes anger. Sartre's account of emotions as unreflective, 'magical' transformations directed at intentional objects explains how fast the insulted fan's world changes, while Heidegger's claim that we are never moodless grounds the idea of a distinct 'Zeppelin mood' that the band's sound articulates better than language could. Schopenhauer's misogynist essay 'On Women' is set beside the song's predatory canine sexuality, and the chapter ends by asking which of the three 'males'—Schopenhauer, Plant's character, or the author with his carefully chosen six-song mix CD—a father could endorse as a son-in-law.

Richard Wilson and Emma Rees apply Freud's theory of fetishism—the boy's disavowal of castration displaced onto a substitute object—to Zeppelin's lyrics and imagery. 'Trampled Underfoot' continues Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues' car-as-lover convention, 'Custard Pie' and 'Black Dog' turn women into consumable food (Freud's cannibalistic pregenital sexual organization), and 'The Lemon Song' and 'Whole Lotta Love' avert the castrating vagina, with the Seattle red snapper episode read through the vagina dentata myth. The band's misogyny ('Soul of a woman was created below' in 'Dazed and Confused', echoing Lear), the voyeuristic die-cut windows of the Physical Graffiti cover, and Plant's cock-rock persona in The Song Remains the Same all illustrate how fetishistic substitution neutralizes the threatening female body and explains the band's compulsive doomed-relationship songs; the authors briefly borrow Marx's language of commodification for the woman-car-drugs as status objects.

chapters.file: ch13 - Singing of the Good Things.md
chapters.relation: Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.

chapters.file: ch14 - True Selves Found or Made.md
chapters.relation: Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.

chapters.file: ch15 - As We Wind on Down the Road.md
chapters.relation: Randall Auxier develops a theory, drawn from Ernst Cassirer's work on myth and magic, that distinguishes magic (the generalizing of will so that past, present, and future connect through symbols and co-operating forces) from myth (the consciousness that experiences the world as wills and archetypal symbols). Page embodies the magical path—the zone musicians enter where playing exceeds conscious control, the Faustian need to master it that led him to Crowley, and the risk of being drained (Page in 1977)—while Plant embodies myth, supplying archetypal lyrics ('The Battle of Evermore', 'Kashmir', 'Stairway' as 'a song of hope') and the Welsh pastoral. Zeppelin's blues borrowing is re-enactment rather than repetition, a rhizome-like reinvention of old roots, and the four unpronounceable symbols of the fourth album are genuine creations: symbols that store concentrated will for the future.

chapters.file: ch16 - I Ain’t Gonna Tell You One Thing that You Really Ought to Know . . . Ooh!.md
chapters.relation: Scott Calef reads the black 'Object' on the Presence cover—which Storm Thorgerson calls not a presence but a hole—to argue that absence permeates Zep's album art (the cut-out wheel of III, the die-cut windows of Physical Graffiti, the spindle holes of Coda) and that holes are a genuine metaphysical puzzle: immaterial yet extended, seemingly causal, and hard to see on a causal theory of perception. Descartes's immaterial soul is compared to holes (both non-physical, though holes suspiciously have size and location), Plato's Forms explain how the Object and we ourselves partake of both Being and Non-Being, and Hume's failure to find a self in introspection makes the self 'a hole'. Kierkegaard and Heidegger connect nothingness to the anxiety of death—fitting an album made after Plant's near-fatal crash—Socrates's two alternatives about death frame the end, and Wittgenstein's 'not a something but not a nothing either' caps the Object's dual nature.

chapters.file: ch17 - Close the Door, Put Out the Lights.md
chapters.relation: Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Eighteenth-century Irish philosopher whose A Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful roots the sublime in self-preservation, terror, and qualities like darkness, vastness, and loudness.
holes.why: Chapter 8's entire analysis of Zeppelin's sublimity—the concert roar, Bonham's drums, 'The Battle of Evermore'—is built on Burke's catalogue of sublime qualities.

holes.name: Longinus
holes.what: Author (c. 1st century AD) of On the Sublime, which treats sublimity as inspired genius whose 'well-timed stroke scatters everything before it like a thunderbolt'.
holes.why: Chapter 8 has a full section using Longinus to explain Plant's flash-of-inspiration writing of 'Stairway to Heaven' and Page's solo as genius rather than recipe.

holes.name: Emergence (collaborative emergence)
holes.what: The idea that group activity can produce novel, unpredictable properties not possessed by any individual component, as in improvised theater or band performance.
holes.why: Chapter 9's positive theory explains Led Zeppelin's creativity as collaborative emergence from the band's interaction, not from any individual genius.

holes.name: Eduard Hanslick
holes.what: Nineteenth-century music critic whose On the Musically Beautiful argued that music's expressiveness lies in dynamically moving form and that the same music can suit opposite words.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central argument—that 'Stairway to Heaven' works with Gilligan's Island lyrics because words and music interact, and that Zeppelin transformed what it borrowed—rests on Hanslick's thought experiment and theory.

holes.name: Mood (Stimmung / Befindlichkeit)
holes.what: Heidegger's notion that we are always already in some mood, which discloses the world as a whole in a particular affective light before any cognition.
holes.why: Chapter 11's thesis that there is a distinct, unnameable 'Zeppelin mood' articulated by the music—and its title concept of a 'Mood Mix'—is directly built on Heidegger's account of mood.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose theory of sexual development includes fetishism, castration anxiety, and the Oedipus complex.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies Freud's fetishism, castration complex, and oral/cannibalistic sexuality to explain Zeppelin's car, food, and body substitutions for the female figure in songs like 'Trampled Underfoot' and 'Custard Pie'.

holes.name: Aleister Crowley
holes.what: Occultist (1875–1947) whose philosophy of Thelema—'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law', magick as will, and the True Will—made him 'the wickedest man in the world'.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is centrally about Crowley's influence on Jimmy Page (Boleskine Manor, the Zoso sigil, the Led Zeppelin III run-out groove) and evaluates Thelema's True Will philosophically.

holes.name: The Perennial Philosophy
holes.what: Aldous Huxley's term for the metaphysical core shared by all mystical religions: a Divine Ground, an eternal Self beyond the phenomenal ego, and union with the Ground as life's purpose.
holes.why: Chapter 14 frames Thelema as an instance of Huxley's perennial philosophy to explain Page's Hermetic quest for self-knowledge through music.

holes.name: Ernst Cassirer
holes.what: Neo-Kantian philosopher (1874–1945) whose philosophy of symbolic forms treats myth and magic as fundamental modes of human thinking from which science and history develop.
holes.why: Chapter 15 states that most of its theory of magic and myth comes from Cassirer's books, using him as the respectable counterpart to Crowley.

holes.name: Symbolic Forms (mythic consciousness)
holes.what: Cassirer's view that humans mediate the world through symbolic forms—myth, language, art, science—with mythic consciousness treating the world as wills and archetypal symbols.
holes.why: Chapter 15 uses symbols as repositories of stored will and mythic consciousness to explain why Plant's archetypal lyrics and the band's album art carry meaning across time.
